report:
**Conclusion:** Your sister’s claim is well supported—particularly for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis who are at high fracture risk.

The key evidence is the 18‑month, randomized, placebo-controlled ACTIVE trial (2,463 women). New vertebral fractures occurred in **0.58%** of women assigned daily subcutaneous abaloparatide versus **4.22%** assigned placebo. That is an absolute reduction of about **3.6 percentage points** and a relative risk reduction of about **86%** (relative risk 0.14; 95% CI 0.05–0.39). The trial also found fewer nonvertebral fractures, though the evidence is strongest for vertebral fractures. [JAMA trial](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640)

The FDA’s prescribing information independently reports the pivotal trial’s vertebral-fracture endpoint and supports its approved use in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high risk of fracture. [FDA label](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/208743lbl.pdf)

Evidence synthesis is consistent with this result: a network meta-analysis concluded that abaloparatide reduces vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk versus placebo and other options in this population. [Meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30953114/)

**Important qualifications:** This is a daily injection and is generally reserved for high/very-high-risk patients, rather than everyone with low bone density. Treatment is time-limited (typically up to two years), and clinicians commonly follow it with an antiresorptive osteoporosis drug to preserve gains. Possible adverse effects include dizziness, nausea, palpitations, and elevated calcium; individual contraindications and risks need clinician review.
